title: 22. Interview: Read Replicas
summary: Interview Q&A for Read Replicas — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Read Replicas interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What problem do read replicas solve and what's the trade-off?
**Answer:** Read replicas solve the **read scaling problem** — when a single primary can't keep up with read traffic, replicas distribute the load horizontally. Most workloads are 10:1 to 100:1 read-to-write, so a primary saturated on reads still has write headroom; adding replicas lets you use that headroom. The trade-off is **eventual consistency**: replicas are updated asynchronously (Topic 13), so they lag the primary by milliseconds to seconds. Reads from replicas may return stale data — a write committed on the primary isn't yet visible on the replica. This creates the **read-after-write problem**: a user writes, then reads their own data from a replica, and sees the old value. Solutions include pinning the user's reads to the primary for N seconds after their write, or always routing the user's own data reads to the primary. The other trade-offs: write throughput is still bounded by the single primary (replicas don't help writes); replication consumes network and replica CPU; failover has a brief downtime (10-60s). Read replicas are the right answer when reads dominate, eventual consistency is acceptable for most queries, and you need horizontal scale without the complexity of sharding. Real-world: Netflix uses ~10 Cassandra replicas for viewing history reads; Amazon Aurora supports up to 15 replicas for catalog reads.
**Visual:**
```
WITHOUT replicas:                WITH replicas:
  reads  -----> Primary            reads  -----> [R1, R2, R3] (scaled)
  writes -----> Primary            writes -----> Primary (only)

  primary saturated on reads       primary handles writes only
  -> slow reads, CPU 100%          replicas handle reads
                                    -> fast reads, primary has headroom

Trade-off: replicas lag primary (ms-sec)
  -> read-after-write: user writes, then reads stale data from replica
  -> fix: pin user's reads to primary for N sec after their write
```

### Q2. What is the read-after-write problem and how do you solve it?
**Answer:** Read-after-write (read-your-writes) is the consistency anomaly where a user writes to the primary, then reads from a replica that hasn't yet received the write — they see stale data. Example: user updates their profile picture (write to primary, 5ms), then the page reloads and reads the profile from a replica with 200ms lag — the replica returns the old picture. The user thinks the update failed. Solutions: (1) **Session pinning** — track `last_write_at` per user session; route that user's reads to the primary for N seconds after their write (N > expected replication lag, typically 5s). Simple and effective for user-facing apps. (2) **Read-your-own-data from primary** — route reads of "my profile," "my cart," "my orders" to the primary always; route reads of "other users' profiles," "product catalog" to replicas. (3) **LSN-based routing** — record the LSN of the user's last write; subsequent reads go to a replica that has caught up to that LSN (PostgreSQL exposes `pg_wal_lsn_diff`). Precise but requires replica LSN tracking. (4) **Client-side cache** — cache the user's own writes locally for N seconds, bypassing the replica. (5) **Synchronous replication** — overkill but eliminates lag; use only for critical data. (6) **Cache-through pattern** — write updates both the primary and a Redis cache; reads hit the cache first (fresh for the user's own data). Real-world: Facebook uses session pinning (30s after a write); Instagram uses Redis for the user's own feed and Cassandra for the durable store.
**Visual:**
```
T=0:  user updates profile (write -> Primary, ack at T=5ms)
T=10: user reloads page (read -> Replica, lag=200ms)
      -> replica applied writes up to T=-190ms
      -> returns OLD profile (stale!)

Fix 1: Session pinning
  after write at T=0, route this user's reads to Primary for 5s
  -> T=10 read goes to Primary, returns new profile (fresh)

Fix 2: Read-your-own-data from primary
  "my profile" -> Primary (always)
  "other's profile" -> Replica (eventual OK)
```

### Q3. How do you route reads to replicas — what strategies exist?
**Answer:** Four common routing strategies: (1) **Round-robin** — distribute reads evenly across replicas in a circular order. Simple, stateless, no replica-specific metrics needed. Bad when replicas have different capacities or lags — a slow replica gets the same traffic as a fast one. (2) **Least-connections** — route to the replica with the fewest active queries. Better load balancing, accounts for query duration differences. Requires a stateful proxy (PgBouncer, ProxySQL, HAProxy) that tracks active connections per replica. (3) **Latency/lag-aware** — route to the replica with the lowest current lag. Useful when lags vary (e.g., one replica is also serving analytics and is behind). Requires the proxy to query replica lag (PostgreSQL `pg_stat_replication`, MySQL `SHOW SLAVE STATUS`). (4) **Workload-based** — classify reads: OLTP queries go to fast replicas; analytical queries go to a dedicated "analytics replica" with more CPU but possibly more lag. The classification can be by query type (SELECT vs aggregate), by user role (admin analytics vs user reads), or by a hint in the connection string. (5) **Geography-based** — route to the geographically nearest replica (cross-region read replicas for global apps). Adds latency-based routing on top of the other strategies. Real-world: PgBouncer supports round-robin and least-connections; AWS Aurora's reader endpoint does round-robin across replicas; Netflix's Cassandra client uses latency-aware routing (token-aware + DynamicEndpointSnitch). The right choice depends on workload heterogeneity — round-robin for uniform replicas, lag-aware for variable replicas, workload-based for mixed read patterns.
**Visual:**
```
ROUND-ROBIN:        LEAST-CONN:         LAG-AWARE:
R1, R2, R3, R1,...  pick fewest conns   pick lowest lag
simple, stateless   stateful proxy      needs lag monitoring
                    better balance      avoids stale replicas

       R1 (lag=50ms, 3 conns)
       R2 (lag=80ms, 1 conn)  <- least-conn picks this
       R3 (lag=200ms, 2 conns)

       lag-aware would pick R1 (lowest lag)
       round-robin would pick R3 (next in rotation)
```

### Q4. How does Amazon Aurora's replication differ from PostgreSQL streaming replication?
**Answer:** Aurora separates compute from storage, fundamentally changing replication. **Traditional PostgreSQL**: each replica has its own storage; the primary streams WAL to replicas, which apply it to their local storage. Replicas lag by milliseconds to seconds depending on network and apply rate. Adding a replica requires copying data (or starting from a backup), taking minutes to hours. **Aurora**: the storage layer is a distributed, replicated log across 6 copies (3 AZs × 2 copies). The primary writes to the storage layer; replicas share the same storage — they don't have their own copy. When a replica needs a page, it reads from the shared storage layer. Replicas have **zero lag** because they read the same data the primary just wrote. Adding a replica is **instant** — no data copy, just a new compute instance pointed at the shared storage. Aurora supports up to 15 read replicas this way. The trade-offs: (1) Aurora is more expensive (6 storage copies, proprietary). (2) Replica compute still costs money (CPU, memory per instance). (3) The shared storage has a quorum-based consistency model (4/6 for writes, 3/6 for reads) — slightly more complex than primary-replica but invisible to users. (4) Aurora replicas still experience replica-level cache misses (the page isn't in their buffer pool yet), so first-read latency can be higher than a warm PostgreSQL replica. Real-world: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL uses traditional streaming replication (lag, slow replica add); Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL uses shared storage (zero lag, instant replicas). Netflix uses Aurora with 10+ replicas for movie metadata.
**Visual:**
```
Traditional PostgreSQL:            Amazon Aurora:
Primary --WAL--> Replica1          Primary ----+
  (each has own storage)           Replica1 ---+---> Shared Storage
Primary --WAL--> Replica2          Replica2 ---+     (6 copies, 3 AZs)
  (lag: ms to sec)                 ...up to 15 replicas
Adding replica: copy data (min-hr) Adding replica: instant (compute only)
                                   Lag: zero (shared storage)
Failover: promote replica          Failover: promote replica (10-30s)
```

### Q5. What is replica lag and how do you monitor and mitigate it?
**Answer:** Replica lag is the time (or bytes of WAL) a replica is behind the primary. Monitoring: PostgreSQL's `pg_stat_replication` view shows `write_lag`, `flush_lag`, `replay_lag` (time-based) and `sent_lsn` vs `replay_lsn` (byte-based). MySQL's `SHOW REPLICA STATUS` shows `Seconds_Behind_Master`. Alert thresholds: >1 second for OLTP replicas (users may notice stale reads), >10 seconds for analytics replicas (acceptable). Causes of growing lag: (1) **Network bottleneck** — bandwidth between primary and replica insufficient for WAL volume. (2) **Replica CPU saturated** — heavy read queries compete with WAL apply. (3) **Single-threaded apply** — old MySQL or PostgreSQL logical replication can't parallelize WAL apply. (4) **Long-running queries on replica** — block apply. (5) **Large transactions** — replica waits for the whole transaction to commit before applying. Mitigations: (1) Scale up the replica (more CPU, faster disk). (2) Move analytical queries to a dedicated replica (not the one serving user reads). (3) Enable parallel WAL apply (MySQL 5.7+, PostgreSQL 14+ logical replication). (4) Batch large transactions into chunks. (5) Use a faster network between primary and replica (within an AZ: 1-2ms; cross-AZ: 5-20ms). (6) For read routing, use lag-aware routing to skip replicas with high lag. (7) For critical reads, fall back to the primary if all replicas are too lagged. Real-world: Slack hit a replica-lag issue and moved heavy queries to a dedicated analytics replica, cutting user-facing replica lag from seconds to milliseconds.
**Visual:**
```
Monitor:
  PG:   SELECT * FROM pg_stat_replication;
        -> write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
        -> sent_lsn, replay_lsn (bytes)
  MySQL: SHOW REPLICA STATUS;
        -> Seconds_Behind_Master

Alert: lag > 1s (OLTP), > 10s (analytics)

Causes:               Mitigations:
  network slow          -> faster network (same-AZ replica)
  replica CPU 100%      -> scale up replica
  single-thread apply   -> parallel apply (MySQL 5.7+, PG 14+)
  long query blocks     -> dedicated analytics replica
  huge transaction      -> batch into chunks

Lag-aware routing: if replica.lag > 1s, route elsewhere
```

### Q6. When should you NOT use read replicas?
**Answer:** Read replicas don't help in several scenarios. (1) **Write-heavy workloads** — if writes are the bottleneck, replicas don't help (they only scale reads). The primary is still the single writer; you need sharding or a multi-leader setup instead. (2) **Strong consistency requirements** — if every read must see the latest write (banking, inventory reservations), you can't use replicas (you'd read from the primary always, defeating the purpose). Use synchronous replication with read-from-primary instead, or accept the latency cost. (3) **Small datasets that fit in RAM** — if the hot working set fits in the primary's buffer pool, reads are already fast (cache hits); replicas add complexity without benefit. (4) **Low read volume** — if reads are 100 QPS, the primary handles them fine; replicas are overkill. (5) **Workloads where caching solves it** — if 90% of reads are to 1% of data (hot products, trending content), a Redis cache is cheaper and faster than replicas. (6) **Write-after-read patterns** — if reads are immediately followed by writes based on the read (read counter, increment, write back), replicas introduce races; use the primary. (7) **Cross-region low-latency reads** — cross-region replicas have 50-200ms lag; a regional cache is often better. (8) **When operational cost outweighs benefit** — replicas double or triple your hardware, monitoring, and failover complexity; if the read scaling isn't needed, skip them. Real-world: many startups over-replicate "for scale" and waste money; the rule of thumb is to add replicas when the primary is at 70%+ CPU on reads. Use caching first (10-100x cheaper), replicas second.
**Visual:**
```
Try in order (cheapest first):
1. Optimize queries + indexes     -- free, big wins
2. Cache hot reads in Redis       -- 10-100x read speedup
3. Add 1 read replica             -- 2x read capacity
4. Add more replicas              -- linear read scale
5. Shard                          -- only when primary is write-bottlenecked

DON'T use replicas when:
  - writes dominate (use sharding)
  - strong consistency required (read from primary)
  - data fits in RAM (cache hits, no I/O benefit)
  - caching solves it (90% reads to 1% data -> Redis)
  - read QPS is low (primary handles it fine)
```

### Q7. How does failover work with read replicas?
**Answer:** When the primary fails, one replica is promoted to be the new primary. Steps: (1) **Failure detection** — a monitoring agent (Patroni, RDS HA, Stolon) pings the primary every 1-5 seconds. After N failures (typically 3-10s of unreachability), it declares the primary down, ideally with quorum consensus (etcd/Consul) to avoid split-brain. (2) **Candidate selection** — pick the replica with the highest LSN (most caught up). If a synchronous replica exists, it's the candidate (zero data loss). With async replicas, pick the one with the smallest lag (minimal data loss). (3) **Promotion** — run `pg_ctl promote` (PostgreSQL) or similar. The replica stops applying WAL, opens for writes, becomes the new primary. Takes 5-30 seconds. (4) **Client rerouting** — update DNS, Consul, or a service discovery endpoint to point at the new primary. PgBouncer/ProxySQL reconnect without client disruption. (5) **Other replicas re-point** — the remaining replicas must now stream from the new primary, not the dead one. Patroni automates this. (6) **Old primary recovery** — when the old primary comes back, it must be re-joined as a replica (not as a primary). This requires fencing — ensuring the old primary isn't accepting writes (split-brain prevention). Patroni uses distributed locks; some setups use STONITH (shoot the other node in the head — power off the old primary). Total downtime: 10-60 seconds. The read replicas continue serving reads throughout failover (they just have a new upstream). Real-world: AWS RDS failover takes 60-120 seconds; Patroni can do 10-30.
**Visual:**
```
T=0:    Primary P fails
T=3s:   Monitoring detects (3 failed pings)
T=5s:   Quorum: P is down (not partition)
T=6s:   Pick candidate: replica with highest LSN (sync replica if any)
T=10s:  pg_ctl promote -> replica is now Primary
T=12s:  Update DNS/Consul -> clients reconnect to new Primary
T=15s:  Writes flow to new Primary; reads to replicas
T=60s:  Old P reboots, fenced, rejoined as replica

Replicas serve reads throughout (different upstream)
Total downtime: 10-60s (write downtime; reads continue)
Data loss: 0 (sync replica) or up to lag of best async replica
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Netflix's movie metadata gets 100k reads/sec but only 100 writes/sec. How do you architect read replicas?
**Answer:** This is a textbook read-replica scenario — 1000:1 read-to-write ratio. I'd use Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the primary handling 100 writes/sec (trivial load) and 10-15 read replicas handling 100k reads/sec distributed via Aurora's reader endpoint (round-robin). Aurora's shared-storage architecture means replicas have zero lag — critical because Netflix's browse page must show consistent metadata (no "I just added a movie to My List, but it's not showing"). For the read-after-write problem (user adds to My List, then reloads), I'd pin that user's reads to the primary for 5 seconds, or use a Redis cache for the user's own My List (write-through: update Aurora + Redis on add, read My List from Redis). The catalog reads (browsing, searching) go to replicas — eventual consistency is fine (a new movie appearing 200ms late in browse is invisible). For global users, I'd add cross-region read replicas in EU and Asia — they have ~100ms lag, acceptable for browse (users in EU see US-catalog updates 100ms late, invisible). Routing: PgBouncer in front of the primary (connection pooling), Aurora reader endpoint for replicas (built-in round-robin), and a Redis layer for hot reads (top-10 trending, recently added) with 5-minute TTL. Cost: 1 primary + 15 replicas is expensive but justified for 100k reads/sec — alternatives (more caching, denormalization) wouldn't eliminate the need for replicas at this scale. Real-world: Netflix actually uses Aurora with 10+ replicas for metadata, EVCache (Redis fork) for hot reads.
**Visual:**
```
Netflix metadata architecture:
  100 writes/sec -> Aurora Primary (1 instance, trivial load)
  100k reads/sec -> 15 Aurora Replicas (zero lag, shared storage)
                    via Aurora reader endpoint (round-robin)

Read-after-write:
  user adds to My List -> write Aurora + Redis (write-through)
  user reads My List   -> Redis (fresh, sub-ms)
  user browses catalog -> Aurora Replica (eventual OK, zero lag anyway)

Global: cross-region replicas in EU/Asia (100ms lag, OK for browse)
Hot reads: Redis cache (top-10 trending, TTL 5min)
```

### Q2. A user reports "I updated my profile but it still shows old data." Diagnose and fix.
**Answer:** Classic read-after-write inconsistency. Diagnosis steps: (1) **Verify the write succeeded** — check the primary for the user's row; is the new value there? If not, the write failed (transaction rolled back, error swallowed). (2) **Check replica lag** — `SELECT * FROM pg_stat_replication` on the primary; what's the lag? If lag is 5 seconds, the user's read from a replica 1 second after the write would see stale data. (3) **Check the read routing** — was the user's read routed to a replica or the primary? If the routing layer doesn't have read-after-write protection, the user's read can hit a stale replica. (4) **Check the user's session** — was the user's read in a new session (no `last_write_at` tracking)? If session state was lost (logout/login, load balancer reroute), the pinning doesn't apply. (5) **Check the cache** — is there a Redis cache layer that wasn't invalidated? A common bug: write updates the DB but not the cache, so reads return cached stale data. Fixes: (1) **Implement session pinning** — track `last_write_at` per session; route the user's reads to the primary for 5 seconds after their write. (2) **Read-your-own-data from primary** — route "my profile" reads to the primary always; route "other's profile" reads to replicas. (3) **Cache invalidation on write** — invalidate the Redis key for the user's profile on write; let the next read repopulate from the primary (or use write-through cache). (4) **Reduce replica lag** — if lag is consistently >1s, scale up replicas or move heavy queries off them. (5) **User-facing mitigation** — show a "saving..." spinner for 1s after the write, masking the lag. Real-world: Facebook had this bug in the early days and implemented 30-second session pinning.
**Visual:**
```
Diagnosis flow:
  1. Write succeeded?  -> check primary for new value
  2. Replica lag?      -> pg_stat_replication
  3. Read routed to?   -> primary or replica?
  4. Session tracked?  -> last_write_at known?
  5. Cache stale?      -> Redis key invalidated?

Fix (in priority order):
  + implement session pinning (5s after write -> primary)
  + read-your-own-data from primary ("my profile" -> primary)
  + invalidate cache on write (or write-through)
  + reduce replica lag (scale up, isolate heavy queries)
  + UX: show "saving..." for 1s after write
```

### Q3. Your primary is at 80% CPU on reads. You add 3 read replicas, but the primary is still at 80%. Why?
**Answer:** The reads aren't being routed to the replicas — they're still hitting the primary. Common causes: (1) **Application not configured to use replicas** — the ORM or connection pooler is sending all queries to the primary. Check the connection string and the read-routing configuration. Django's `DATABASE_ROUTERS`, SQLAlchemy's `Session(bind=...)`, Hibernate's `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` need to be set up correctly. (2) **Read-only transactions not marked as such** — PostgreSQL routes queries within `BEGIN READ ONLY` to replicas (if using pgpool or a smart router); without the marker, they go to the primary. The app must explicitly mark read-only transactions. (3) **Cross-transaction state** — a single connection that did a write earlier in the session might continue routing reads to the primary (sticky routing). Pooler must reset this state between requests. (4) **The reads ARE going to replicas, but the primary is also doing extra work** — WAL shipping to 3 replicas adds CPU load to the primary (sending WAL over the network). At high write rates, this can be significant. Check `pg_stat_replication` and the primary's network/CPU. (5) **Long-running queries on the primary** — a single analytical query on the primary (perhaps run by an admin) can pin CPU at 80%. Check `pg_stat_activity` for slow queries. (6) **Replica reads failing and falling back to the primary** — if the router tries replicas and they time out or error, it falls back to the primary. Check replica health. (7) **Cache miss cascades** — if the cache layer is failing, all reads bypass it and hit the DB. Fixes: verify routing config, mark read-only transactions, isolate analytical queries, monitor replica health, and ensure the cache layer is working. Real-world: this is the most common misconfiguration — replicas exist but aren't being used.
**Visual:**
```
Primary CPU 80% even with 3 replicas? Diagnose:

  1. App routing config?       -> DATABASE_ROUTERS, Session(bind=...)
  2. Read-only marked?         -> BEGIN READ ONLY; SELECT ...
  3. Sticky session?           -> pooler not resetting state
  4. WAL shipping overhead?    -> 3 replicas = 3x WAL send CPU
  5. Long query on primary?    -> pg_stat_activity
  6. Replica reads failing?    -> fallback to primary
  7. Cache miss cascade?       -> cache layer down?

Fix:
  + configure ORM to route reads to replicas
  + mark read-only transactions
  + isolate analytical queries to dedicated replica
  + monitor replica health, no fallback-to-primary on read
```

### Q4. You have a global app with users in US, EU, Asia. Reads should be fast (sub-50ms) for everyone. How do you architect?
**Answer:** Cross-region read replicas in each region, with the primary in one region (or multi-master). Architecture: (1) **Primary in us-east-1** (largest user base, lowest write latency for the most users). (2) **Cross-region read replicas in eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-1** — async replication, ~100-200ms lag. (3) **Geography-based routing** — Route 53 or a global load balancer routes users to the nearest region's replica for reads. Sub-50ms read latency for everyone. (4) **Writes go to the primary** — write latency is 100-300ms for EU/Asia users (cross-region to us-east-1). Acceptable for most apps; for write-heavy global apps, use multi-master (CockroachDB, Spanner, DynamoDB Global Tables). (5) **Read-after-write handling** — for users who just wrote, route their next reads to the primary (cross-region, slow but consistent) OR use a local cache (Redis in each region, write-through on write, TTL 5s). The cache returns fresh data for the user's own writes without a cross-region read. (6) **Eventual consistency for global data** — a US user's profile update is visible to EU users after ~200ms (replication lag). Acceptable for most features (social feed, comments); not acceptable for financial data. (7) **Multi-region active-active for write-heavy** — if writes are global and latency-critical, use CockroachDB or DynamoDB Global Tables (multi-master with conflict resolution). The trade-off: conflict resolution complexity (LWW, CRDTs). Real-world: Netflix deploys regionally (US, EU, Asia) with Cassandra clusters in each, async replication between them — viewing history is regional, global catalog is read-replicated; Amazon uses DynamoDB Global Tables for shopping carts (multi-master, CRDT-like).
**Visual:**
```
Global read architecture:
  US users  -> us-east-1 replica (sub-50ms read)
  EU users  -> eu-west-1 replica (sub-50ms read)
  Asia users-> ap-southeast-1 replica (sub-50ms read)
  All writes-> us-east-1 primary (100-300ms for EU/Asia)

  Primary (us-east-1) --async repl--> eu-west-1 replica (~100ms lag)
                     \--async repl--> ap-southeast-1 replica (~150ms lag)

Read-after-write:
  EU user writes -> primary (us-east-1, 200ms)
  EU user reads  -> local Redis cache (write-through, fresh) OR primary
  EU user reads other data -> eu-west-1 replica (sub-50ms, eventual)

Multi-master (if write latency critical):
  CockroachDB / DynamoDB Global Tables / Spanner
  -> conflict resolution (LWW, CRDTs)
```

### Q5. You need to run a heavy analytical query (10-minute aggregation) on production data. How do you avoid impacting users?
**Answer:** Run it on a dedicated analytics replica, not the primary or user-facing replicas. Architecture: (1) **Add a dedicated "analytics replica"** — a read replica with more CPU and RAM, specifically for analytical queries. Don't share it with user-facing reads. (2) **Route analytical queries to it** — the BI tool, dashboard, or ad-hoc analyst connects to the analytics replica's endpoint, not the primary or user replicas. (3) **Accept higher replica lag** — the analytics replica might lag the primary by seconds to minutes (because heavy analytical queries compete with WAL apply). For analytics, this is fine — a dashboard showing data 5 seconds old is acceptable. (4) **Use a connection pooler with separate pools** — even on the analytics replica, separate the BI tool's pool from ad-hoc analyst queries, so a runaway query doesn't block others. (5) **Throttle the query** — use `statement_timeout` to kill queries that run too long; use `max_parallel_workers` to limit CPU usage. (6) **Materialize the result** — if the same query runs repeatedly (e.g., daily dashboard refresh), materialize it: a scheduled job runs the aggregation overnight into a summary table, and the dashboard reads the summary (fast). (7) **Use a separate analytics warehouse** — for true analytical workloads (terabytes, complex joins, full-table scans), replicate to a columnar warehouse (BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake) via CDC. The warehouse is designed for analytics; the OLTP database is not. Real-world: Netflix uses Redshift/Snowflake for analytics, with CDC from Cassandra/PostgreSQL; the operational databases never see analytical queries.
**Visual:**
```
Avoid running analytics on primary or user replicas:

  Primary          -> writes only (don't touch)
  User Replicas    -> user reads (don't slow them down)
  Analytics Replica -> BI tools, dashboards, ad-hoc
                        (dedicated, more CPU, accepts lag)

For heavy analytics (TB-scale, complex joins):
  Operational DB --CDC--> Columnar Warehouse (Redshift/BigQuery)
                           -> runs the 10-min aggregation
                           -> operational DB untouched

Best practice: materialize daily summaries
  nightly job: INSERT INTO daily_summary SELECT ... FROM raw WHERE date=yesterday
  dashboard: SELECT * FROM daily_summary WHERE date=today (fast)
```

### Q6. A replica's lag is growing unboundedly (1s, 5s, 30s, 2min). What's happening and what do you do?
**Answer:** Unbounded lag means the replica can't keep up with the primary's WAL stream. Immediate actions: (1) **Check the replica's CPU and I/O** — is it saturated? If so, scale up (more CPU, faster disk) or move heavy queries off it. (2) **Check for long-running queries on the replica** — `pg_stat_activity` for queries with old `query_start`. A single slow query can block WAL apply (in single-threaded mode). Kill it (`pg_terminate_backend`). (3) **Check for huge transactions on the primary** — a single `DELETE FROM million_row_table` produces a massive WAL entry; the replica must wait for the entire transaction to commit before applying. Identify with `pg_stat_activity` on the primary. (4) **Check the network** — is bandwidth between primary and replica saturated? `iftop` or CloudWatch metrics. (5) **Check for locks on the replica** — `pg_locks` for granted locks that block apply. While diagnosing, mitigate user impact: (a) **Remove the replica from the read rotation** — route its reads to other replicas or the primary; don't serve stale reads. (b) **Alert and page** — at >1s lag, users may notice; at >30s, the replica is unusable. (c) **Consider rebuilding the replica** — if lag is unbounded and the cause isn't obvious, it may be faster to drop the replica and rebuild from a snapshot (takes minutes to hours, but produces a clean state). Long-term fixes: (a) Scale up the replica; (b) enable parallel WAL apply (PG 14+); (c) batch large transactions on the primary; (d) isolate heavy queries to a dedicated replica; (e) use logical replication with table filtering to reduce WAL volume. Real-world: this is a common ops issue; the standard playbook is "pull from rotation, diagnose, scale up, re-add when caught up."
**Visual:**
```
Replica lag growing (1s -> 5s -> 30s -> 2min):

Immediate:
  1. Check CPU/IO (saturated? -> scale up)
  2. Check long-running queries on replica (pg_stat_activity -> kill)
  3. Check huge transactions on primary (DELETE million rows?)
  4. Check network bandwidth
  5. Check locks on replica (pg_locks)

Mitigate user impact:
  - pull replica from read rotation
  - alert/page at >1s lag
  - rebuild from snapshot if unfixable (last resort)

Long-term:
  + scale up replica
  + parallel WAL apply (PG 14+)
  + batch large transactions on primary
  + isolate heavy queries to dedicated replica
  + logical replication with table filtering
```

### Q7. You're using Amazon Aurora with 10 replicas. A user complains that their write appears then disappears. Why?
**Answer:** This is a classic "lagging replica after failover" or "round-robin routing during failover" issue. With 10 Aurora replicas and round-robin routing via the Aurora reader endpoint, a user's request may hit different replicas on each call. Scenario: (1) User writes (primary, succeeds). (2) User reads (replica A, hasn't replicated yet — sees old data). (3) User reloads (replica B, has replicated — sees new data). (4) User reloads again (replica A still hasn't replicated due to a transient lag — sees old data). The data "appears then disappears" because different replicas have different lag. Even though Aurora replicas share storage (zero lag in theory), cache warming and buffer pool differences can cause sub-second lag in practice. Fixes: (1) **Session pinning** — pin the user to a single replica for the duration of their session (or for N seconds after a write). The user always reads from the same replica, so they see monotonic progress (once a replica has the write, it always has it). PgBouncer or a smart client can do this with sticky sessions. (2) **Read-after-write pinning to the primary** — for N seconds after the user's write, route all their reads to the primary (zero lag, fresh data). (3) **Read-your-own-data from primary** — "my data" reads always go to the primary; "others' data" reads go to replicas. (4) **Cache the user's writes** — Redis write-through cache; the user's own reads hit Redis (fresh), bypassing the replica lag issue. (5) **Use Aurora's consistent reader endpoint** — Aurora Reader endpoint can be configured with consistency-aware routing. The root cause is round-robin routing across replicas with non-uniform lag; the fix is to make the user's reads monotonic (same replica or primary). Real-world: AWS docs explicitly call out this issue and recommend session-based replica selection for read-after-write scenarios.
**Visual:**
```
Round-robin across 10 replicas:
  T=0:  write -> Primary (ok)
  T=1:  read  -> Replica A (lag=200ms, returns OLD)   <- "appears gone"
  T=2:  read  -> Replica B (lag=0, returns NEW)       <- "appears"
  T=3:  read  -> Replica A (lag=200ms, returns OLD)   <- "disappears"

Fix 1: Session pinning (sticky to one replica)
  -> user always reads from Replica B (or whichever was first)
  -> monotonic: once B has it, B always has it

Fix 2: Read-after-write pinning to primary (5s)
  -> after write, user reads from Primary (zero lag)

Fix 3: Read-your-own-data from primary always
  -> "my data" reads -> Primary; "others'" reads -> Replicas
```
